In April 1815 Mount Tambora, a volcano on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, erupted in the most powerful volcanic eruption in recorded history. It peaked on 10 April and threw some 37 to 45 cubic kilometres of rock and ash into the air.

Explosions were heard more than 2,000 km away. Ash and pyroclastic flows buried villages, and the small kingdom of Tambora was wiped out. On Sumbawa and the nearby island of Lombok tens of thousands of people died, most from famine and disease after the ash destroyed crops. Java was then under brief British rule, and the lieutenant-governor, Stamford Raffles, collected reports of the disaster.

The ash and sulphur spread around the world and cooled the climate. The next year, 1816, became the Year Without a Summer:

  • Snow fell in New England in June, and frosts killed crops through the summer.
  • Harvests failed across Europe, bringing food riots and hunger, and a wave of emigration from Germany and New England.
  • In China's Yunnan province cold summers ruined the rice crop and caused famine.
  • Kept indoors by storms on Lake Geneva, Mary Shelley began Frankenstein.

Some historians link the disrupted monsoon to the cholera outbreak in Bengal in 1817, though the connection is not proven. At the time almost no one tied the cold to a volcano in the Dutch East Indies. Tambora is still the most recent confirmed eruption of its size, far larger than the better known Krakatoa eruption of 1883.
